## Chapter 2 — VOLC ENSO

### timmreck2024linearity
**Timmreck, C., Güll, M., Poberaj, C.S., Jungclaus, J.H. et al. (2024).** Linearity of the climate response to increasingly strong tropical volcanic eruptions in a large ensemble framework. *Journal of Climate*, 37, 2455–2470. https://doi.org/10.1175/JCLI-D-23-0408.1

**Why relevant:** Tests whether temperature and precipitation responses scale linearly with eruption magnitude in a large ensemble. Directly informs interpretation of Ch2's 0.5×/0.75×/1× seasonal-scaling spaghetti plots — if the climate system responds nonlinearly, then scaling eruption forcing doesn't simply scale the ENSO response.

**Key finding:** Linear scaling holds for temperature at most latitudes; precipitation and circulation responses (including ENSO teleconnections) show measurable nonlinearities at the high end of eruption magnitude. This supports Ch2's hypothesis that there is a nonlinear threshold in ENSO amplitude response.

## Chapter 3 — California-VOLC-ENSO

### todd2025drought
**Todd, V.L., Shanahan, T.M., DiNezio, P.N., Klavans, J.M., Fawcett, P.J., Anderson, R.S., Jiménez-Moreno, G., LeGrande, A.N., Pausata, F.S.R., Thompson, A.J., Zhu, J. (2025).** North Pacific ocean–atmosphere responses to Holocene and future warming drive Southwest US drought. *Nature Geoscience*, 18(7), 646–652. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41561-025-01726-z

**Why relevant:** Identifies two distinct pathways linking North Pacific conditions to Southwest US drought — one ENSO-mediated, one via direct storm-track adjustment. Ch3 argues volcanic forcing affects California hydroclimate via ENSO modulation; this paper adds a secondary pathway (North Pacific storm-track suppression) that could amplify the volcanic signal even if the ENSO response is weak.

**Key finding:** Under warming, a weakened Aleutian Low and shifted storm track reduce Southwest US precipitation independently of ENSO. Post-eruption cooling could partially suppress this mechanism, complicating attribution of volcanic→California drought to a single ENSO-only pathway.

## Chapter 4 — Biogeochem & Geo Fish

### galloso2025ensofish
**Galloso, P., Correa, G.M., Legendre, P. (2025).** The impacts of El Niño Southern Oscillation on the pelagic fish community structure of the northern Humboldt Current system. *Deep Sea Research Part II: Topical Studies in Oceanography*. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dsr2.2025.105553

**Why relevant:** Provides empirical community-composition data showing ENSO phase directly reshapes fish diversity in the northern HCS. Complements the habitat-compression framing ([@enso2025aerobic]) and metabolic-index predictability work ([@scott2025metabolic]) already in Ch4.

**Key finding:** El Niño increases pelagic fish diversity via expanded warm oxygenated habitat; La Niña decreases diversity via OMZ shoaling. Response scales with ENSO intensity, establishing the full causal chain: ENSO state → biogeochemical anomaly → habitat structure → community composition.

## Chapter 5 — Climate Tech Sentiment

### nawaz2025community
**Nawaz, S., Belotti, G. (2025).** Community perspectives on marine carbon dioxide removal and ocean alkalinity enhancement: A future scenario approach. *Energy Research & Social Science*. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.erss.2025.104080

**Why relevant:** Community workshops in Sequim, WA on OAE document public preferences for existing infrastructure, minimal coastline industrialization, and community/Tribal ownership models. Contextualizes Ch5's GDELT/VADER sentiment findings — the positive OAE media tone may diverge significantly from ground-level community ambivalence documented here.

**Key finding:** Participants generally open to OAE under conditions of local control and co-design; concerns center on scale and industrialization rather than the chemistry itself. This community–media sentiment gap is analytically important for Ch5.
